artifacts.title: PCP Referral Note
artifacts.author: Dr. R. Nguyen, Internal Medicine
artifacts.body: 45-year-old male with dyslipidemia (LDL 195, HDL 30, TG 180), prediabetes (A1c 5.8%, FBG 110), and essential hypertension (BP 148/92 on lisinopril 20mg). Family history of early CAD. Started atorvastatin 40mg six months ago; patient reports some improvement but lipids remain significantly elevated. Referring to registered dietitian for medical nutrition therapy and lifestyle counseling given elevated cardiovascular risk. Will recheck lipid panel in 3 months. Please address dietary pattern, physical activity, and discuss medication adherence as part of comprehensive risk reduction plan.

facts.chart: Referred by PCP for MNT for dyslipidemia, prediabetes, and hypertension
facts.says: My doctor sent me here because my cholesterol is too high, I guess.

facts.chart: Works as an airplane mechanic, long shifts
facts.says: I'm a mechanic, work on aircraft. Long shifts, 10-12 hours sometimes.

facts.chart: 45-year-old married male
facts.says: I'm 45, married, got a couple kids at home.

facts.chart: Lives with spouse and young children
facts.says: My wife and the kids are home with me, yeah.

facts.chart: Reports eating 3 meals a day, though breakfast often skipped
facts.says: I eat three times a day, more or less. Sometimes I skip breakfast if I'm running late.

facts.chart: Heavy dinner, often fast food or convenience food - burgers, pizza
facts.says: Dinner's the big meal. Burger and fries, pizza, whatever's quick after a long shift.

facts.chart: Low fruit and vegetable intake, roughly 1 serving/day or less
facts.says: Vegetables? Man, I don't really do salads. Maybe some corn or something once in a while.

facts.chart: Drinks soda regularly, inadequate plain water intake
facts.says: I'll grab a soda with lunch and dinner most days. Water's not really my thing.

facts.chart: Grills meats on weekends, often processed/fatty cuts
facts.says: Weekends I like to grill out - burgers, ribs, sausage links. That's my thing with the guys.

facts.chart: Reports drinking beer most evenings, heavier on weekends while watching football
facts.says: I'll have a few beers watching the game, maybe 4 or 5 on a Saturday. During the week, maybe one or two.

facts.chart: Sedentary; minimal structured exercise, long work shifts limit movement
facts.says: I'm on my feet at work but it's not really exercise. Honestly I just want to sit down when I get home.

facts.chart: Irregular sleep due to shift work, often under 6 hours
facts.says: My sleep's all over the place with the shifts. Some nights I only get 5, 6 hours.

facts.chart: Reports dizziness attributed to atorvastatin
facts.says: That cholesterol pill makes me feel kind of dizzy sometimes, lightheaded.

facts.chart: Admits to skipping atorvastatin doses several times a week due to perceived side effects
facts.says: I don't take it every single day, honestly. If I feel off I just skip it. Maybe I miss it three, four times a week.

facts.chart: Reports persistent dry cough since starting lisinopril, has not reported to PCP
facts.says: I've had this dry cough ever since I started the blood pressure pill. Haven't said anything to the doctor about it.

facts.chart: Takes lisinopril consistently as prescribed
facts.says: That one I take every morning, no problem, no missed days.

facts.chart: Believes statins cause muscle pain/damage and are unnecessary long-term
facts.says: I read online statins eat away at your muscles. I don't want to be on something like that forever.

facts.chart: Limited understanding of what LDL/HDL numbers mean or imply for risk
facts.says: They just tell me the numbers but honestly I don't really know what's good or bad.

facts.chart: Perceives healthy eating as too expensive and inconvenient given his schedule
facts.says: Eating healthy costs more and takes more time than I've got most days.

facts.chart: Reports approximately 16 lb weight gain over the past year, attributes to long shifts and convenience eating
facts.says: I guess I've put on some weight this past year. Probably 15, 16 pounds. The shifts don't help.

facts.chart: Father had heart attack at age 50; strong family history of early coronary artery disease
facts.says: My dad had a heart attack when he was 50. That's actually what scares me a little.

facts.chart: Primary motivation is to avoid a heart attack and remain active with grandchildren and at work
facts.says: I don't want to end up like my dad. And I want to keep working, play with my grandkids someday.

facts.chart: Resistant to being told what to eat; prefers practical, autonomy-respecting suggestions
facts.says: I don't need somebody telling me I can't eat anything I like. Just give me something that actually works.

facts.chart: Spouse encourages healthier eating but has limited direct involvement in his meals due to his schedule
facts.says: My wife's always on me to eat better. She tries, but with my hours we don't always eat together.

facts.chart: History of severe migraines, not currently active, unrelated to current visit
facts.says: I used to get bad migraines a few years back. Not really an issue lately.

facts.chart: No known food or medication allergies
facts.says: No allergies that I know of.

facts.chart: Non-smoker, never smoked
facts.says: Never smoked, no.

facts.chart: Takes fish oil, vitamin D3, and a multivitamin daily, started on his own
facts.says: I take fish oil and vitamin D and a multivitamin. Figured it couldn't hurt.

facts.chart: Reports large portion sizes at dinner, often eating until full/uncomfortable
facts.says: I eat till I'm full, sometimes past full honestly after a long shift.

facts.chart: Reports work stress related to physically demanding shifts and fear of losing job if health declines
facts.says: If my health gets bad enough I can't do the job, that scares me more than anything.

facts.chart: Denies chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations currently
facts.says: No chest pain, no trouble breathing, nothing like that right now.

facts.chart: Rarely cooks from scratch; relies on spouse or takeout for most non-grilled meals
facts.says: I'm not much of a cook myself, outside of grilling. My wife handles most of it, or we just grab something.

facts.chart: Expresses some openness to making dietary changes if practical and not overly restrictive
facts.says: I could probably do some things different with eating, if it's not some crazy diet.

facts.chart: Worried about ongoing cost of medications long-term
facts.says: These pills aren't cheap either, and that's forever if I stay on them.

patient.name: Omar Sinclair
patient.appearance: Joining by video from his kitchen table on a day off, still in a work polo. Solid build, direct eye contact, arms crossed at first, relaxes somewhat as rapport builds. Keeps a can of soda nearby.

persona.personality: Independent, skeptical, practical, resistant to being told what to do, protective of his autonomy but genuinely cares about his family
persona.communicationStyle: Direct and concise; answers questions briefly at first; dislikes lectures; responds better to practical, specific suggestions than general advice; uses plain language
persona.emotionalState: Guarded and a little defensive initially, especially about medications; opens up when he feels heard rather than judged; underlying worry about his father's heart attack
persona.background: Omar has worked as an aircraft mechanic for over 20 years, often pulling long 10-12 hour shifts. He's married with young kids at home and values being able to provide and stay physically capable for his job. He grills with neighbors on weekends and watches football, which is a big part of his social life. He takes pride in being self-reliant and fixing things himself - he approaches his health the same way, preferring to just 'make an adjustment' rather than being on medication forever.
speechExamples: Look, I don't have time for some fancy diet plan.
My cholesterol's high, fine, but I feel fine, so I don't get what the big deal is.
I'm not trying to be on five different pills by the time I'm fifty.
If you give me something practical I can actually do, I'm listening.
My dad died of a heart attack at fifty. That's really why I'm here, if I'm honest.
concerns: Medication side effects, especially the dizziness from the statin
Being told to give up foods he enjoys
Not fully understanding what his lab numbers mean
Being judged for his eating habits

scenario.studentBrief: You are seeing Omar Sinclair, a 45-year-old aircraft mechanic, for a telehealth nutrition assessment following a PCP referral for medical nutrition therapy for dyslipidemia and related cardiometabolic risk. His chart shows dyslipidemia, prediabetes, and hypertension. Conduct a nutrition assessment and use motivational interviewing to begin building a plan he can realistically follow.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Referral for medical nutrition therapy for dyslipidemia and related cardiometabolic risk
scenario.openingLine: Hey, yeah, I'm Omar. My doctor said I need to talk to a dietitian because of my cholesterol numbers. Not really sure what you can tell me that I don't already know, but go ahead.
tasks: Conduct a thorough nutrition-focused diet history and identify barriers to healthy eating
Review relevant labs, vitals, and anthropometrics to complete the nutrition assessment
Explore lifestyle factors that may impact nutrition care
Take a focused history of medication use and any concerns
Collaborate with Omar using motivational interviewing to set one or two realistic, patient-centered nutrition goals

objectives.text: Apply the Nutrition Care Process by completing a comprehensive assessment integrating diet history, anthropometrics, labs, and medication/lifestyle factors
Develop an accurate PES statement linking elevated LDL/low HDL to excessive saturated fat intake, low fiber/produce intake, and sedentary pattern, with the effect being increased cardiovascular risk
Identify and explore the discrepancy between Omar's report of inconsistent statin use and the pharmacy refill record, addressing it non-judgmentally
Use motivational interviewing techniques to explore Omar's readiness to change, values, and barriers rather than prescribing a rigid diet plan
Address lifestyle and behavioral barriers (cost, convenience, shift work, alcohol use) and collaboratively identify realistic, specific nutrition goals
Recognize the need for interprofessional coordination, including communicating medication side-effect concerns back to the PCP rather than adjusting medications directly

answerKey.primaryProblem: Excessive saturated fat and inadequate fiber/produce intake contributing to atherogenic dyslipidemia (elevated LDL, low HDL, elevated triglycerides) in a patient with prediabetes and hypertension and significant cardiovascular risk factors
differential: Primary nutrition diagnosis: Excessive fat intake (saturated fat) related to frequent consumption of fast food, processed/grilled meats and irregular meal pattern, as evidenced by elevated LDL 195 mg/dL and total cholesterol 260 mg/dL
Secondary: Inadequate fiber/fruit-vegetable intake related to limited access/convenience and low health literacy, as evidenced by reported near-absence of fruit/vegetable intake
Secondary: Excessive alcohol intake related to social/weekend drinking pattern, as evidenced by AUDIT-C score of 5 and reported 4-5 drinks several times weekly
Contributing: Medication nonadherence (statin) related to perceived side effects and low health literacy about cardiovascular risk, as evidenced by refill gaps and self-report of missed doses
keyFindings: LDL 195 mg/dL, HDL 30 mg/dL, Total cholesterol 260 mg/dL, Triglycerides 180 mg/dL - atherogenic dyslipidemia
BMI 29.2 and waist circumference 43 in - increased cardiometabolic risk, central adiposity
HbA1c 5.8% and fasting glucose 110 mg/dL - prediabetes
~16 lb weight gain over past year tied to shift-work eating pattern
Reported statin nonadherence (missing ~3-4 doses/week) corroborated by pharmacy refill gaps
Minimal fruit/vegetable intake, heavy reliance on fast food/processed/grilled meats, regular soda intake
AUDIT-C score 5 indicating risky alcohol consumption, previously undisclosed
Low health literacy regarding lipid panel interpretation and cardiovascular risk
plan: Complete ADIME note: Assessment summarizing diet history, anthropometrics, labs, and psychosocial/MI findings; PES statement(s) as above; Intervention negotiated collaboratively with patient; Monitoring/Evaluation plan for follow-up

Negotiate 1-2 specific, achievable goals (e.g., adding one vegetable serving at dinner, swapping one soda per day for water, choosing leaner grilled proteins on weekends) rather than prescribing a full diet overhaul
Address alcohol intake using MI approach, provide brief feedback on AUDIT-C score and cardiovascular/triglyceride implications
Communicate statin dizziness/adherence concern and lisinopril-associated dry cough to PCP for medication review; emphasize dietitian is not adjusting medications directly
Provide brief, plain-language education on what LDL/HDL/triglycerides mean and why they matter for his specific goal of avoiding his father's outcome
Discuss practical, lower-cost strategies for produce access and meal planning given shift-work schedule and stated cost barrier
Schedule follow-up nutrition visit before PCP's 3-month lipid recheck to assess progress on goals
Involve spouse where feasible as support system, respecting his autonomy and schedule constraints
redFlags: BP 148/92 mmHg is above goal and should be flagged for PCP follow-up given hypertension diagnosis
Unreported dry cough on lisinopril should be relayed to PCP (possible ACE-inhibitor side effect)
AUDIT-C score of 5 suggests risky drinking that may be exacerbating triglycerides and warrants further screening/referral
Statin nonadherence pattern should be communicated to PCP, not resolved by the dietitian independently adjusting medication
educationPoints: Explain LDL, HDL, and triglycerides in plain language and relate them concretely to his father's heart attack and his goal of staying active for his family
Clarify that statin-associated muscle concerns are a known but manageable issue to discuss with his prescriber, and that stopping or skipping doses without guidance leaves LDL uncontrolled
Reinforce that dietary change can meaningfully lower LDL and triglycerides and may reduce how much medication he ultimately needs, appealing to his preference for self-reliant solutions
Teach practical, low-cost strategies for incorporating vegetables and fiber within a shift-work schedule and grilling-based social eating
Normalize that moderate alcohol intake raises triglycerides and can blunt cardiovascular benefits of other changes, without being punitive or judgmental
Emphasize the dietitian's role is collaborative goal-setting, not restriction, aligning with his stated preference for practical, non-lecturing guidance

mismatches.patientClaim: Omar reports missing his atorvastatin roughly 3-4 times per week due to feeling dizzy, but frames it as occasional/minor when first asked.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy refill history shows atorvastatin 90-day supplies being refilled 2-3 weeks late on the last two refill cycles, consistent with substantial missed doses, while lisinopril refills are consistently on time.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Self-reported adherence often underestimates true nonadherence; refill gap analysis is an objective way to corroborate (or gently challenge) a patient's adherence report without being accusatory, and should prompt a non-judgmental MI-style conversation plus communication to the prescriber.

profile.summary: Omar Sinclair is a 45-year-old aircraft mechanic with dyslipidemia (LDL 195, HDL 30), prediabetes, and hypertension, referred for medical nutrition therapy. The case trains dietetics students to complete a Nutrition Care Process assessment, uncover hidden barriers (alcohol use, low produce intake, statin nonadherence corroborated by refill records) through progressive disclosure, and apply motivational interviewing with a skeptical, pragmatic patient who is more contemplative about diet than medication.
profile.title: Dyslipidemia and Medication Skepticism in a 45-Year-Old Aircraft Mechanic
